title: Implanted Port (Port-a-Cath) Access
summary: Accessing and maintaining a subcutaneous implanted venous access port for chemotherapy or long-term IV therapy.
steps: Palpate the port septum through the skin — identify the center and edges of the port body.
Perform hand hygiene. Open sterile field. Don sterile gloves.
Clean the skin over the port with chlorhexidine — scrub for 30 seconds, allow to dry 30 seconds.
Stabilize the port with non-dominant hand, holding it between thumb and first two fingers.
Insert the Huber needle perpendicular to the port septum, pushing firmly until you feel the needle hit the back of the port reservoir.
NEVER use a standard bevel needle — it will core the silicone septum and destroy the port.
Aspirate for blood return to confirm placement. If no return: flush with 10mL NS, reposition patient (arm overhead, deep breath), try aspirating again.
Flush with 10mL NS using turbulent (push-pause) technique.
Apply transparent dressing. Secure Huber needle tubing to skin.
Deaccess: flush with 10mL NS then heparin lock (100 units/mL per policy). Withdraw needle while maintaining positive pressure.
safetyTips: Only Huber needles may access an implanted port — regular needles core the septum and cause permanent damage.
No blood return despite correct needle position: flush and reposition — a fibrin sheath may be present. Notify provider if unresolved.
Accidental dislodgement of a port needle during infusion = extravasation of chemotherapy. Stop infusion immediately.

title: Chemotherapy Safe Handling & Administration
summary: Safely preparing, administering, and disposing of hazardous chemotherapy agents (NIOSH hazardous drugs).
equipment: Chemotherapy-designated PPE: double gloves (chemo-rated), gown (water-resistant, long sleeves, closed front), face shield
Closed system transfer device (CSTD) if applicable
steps: Verify chemotherapy orders per protocol: name, dose in mg/m² or mg/kg, route, cycle/day, required premedications.
Confirm BSA (body surface area) or weight calculation matches the dose ordered.
Two-nurse verification required: drug, dose, route, rate, patient ID.
Don PPE: double gloves (check for pinholes), gown, face shield. Don gown first, then outer gloves over gown cuffs.
Inspect the prepared bag for clarity, color, precipitation, label accuracy.
Administer premedications (antiemetics, corticosteroids, hydration) as ordered.
Verify IV access patency — blood return required for vesicant agents.
Infuse per order. Monitor IV site every 15–30 minutes for vesicants (extravasation risk).
Post-infusion: flush line per protocol. Doff PPE in correct order.
Dispose of all supplies in chemotherapy waste container. Do NOT place in regular trash.
Chemotherapy spill kit must be at bedside. If spill occurs: don PPE, contain spill with kit, clean per policy, complete incident report.
safetyTips: Chemotherapy is a hazardous drug — absorb through skin/mucous membranes. PPE is not optional.
Vesicant extravasation is an oncologic emergency — stop infusion, aspirate residual, notify provider, apply cold or warm compress per vesicant type.
Pregnant nurses should NOT administer chemotherapy — teratogenic risk.

title: Blood Transfusion Reaction Recognition & Response
summary: Recognizing acute transfusion reactions and initiating the correct response.
steps: Monitor patient at bedside for the FIRST 15 MINUTES of each unit — most acute reactions occur here.
FEBRILE NON-HEMOLYTIC REACTION (most common): fever >1°C rise, chills, no hemolysis. Stop transfusion, notify provider, give antipyretics, may resume with pre-medication.
ALLERGIC REACTION (urticaria): hives, pruritis. Stop transfusion, give diphenhydramine, notify provider. May resume if mild urticaria resolves.
ANAPHYLAXIS: bronchospasm, hypotension, angioedema. STOP transfusion, 911/RRT, epinephrine 0.3mg IM, O2, IV fluids. Do NOT restart.
ACUTE HEMOLYTIC REACTION (most dangerous): fever, chills, flank/back pain, dark urine (hemoglobinuria), hypotension. STOP immediately — ABO incompatibility.
TRANSFUSION-RELATED ACUTE LUNG INJURY (TRALI): acute onset respiratory failure within 6h. Stop, O2, supportive care, notify provider.
FOR ALL REACTIONS: Stop transfusion. Maintain IV with NS using NEW tubing. Obtain vital signs. Notify provider. Send blood bag and new blood sample to blood bank.
Complete incident report. Document all interventions and patient response.
safetyTips: Sending the blood bag back to the blood bank is critical — they must verify the unit against the patient's sample.
Back and flank pain during transfusion = hemolytic reaction until proven otherwise — stop immediately.
TACO (Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload): dyspnea, hypertension, bilateral crackles. More common in elderly/heart failure. Slow rate or stop; diuresis.
keyTakeaways: Stop transfusion for ANY suspected reaction
Keep IV open with NS via NEW tubing

title: IV Extravasation & Infiltration Management
summary: Recognizing and managing IV extravasation (vesicant) and infiltration (non-vesicant) to minimize tissue damage.
equipment: Antidote per drug protocol (hyaluronidase, sodium thiosulfate, phentolamine, DMSO)
Warm or cold compress per protocol
steps: IDENTIFY: Infiltration (non-vesicant) = swelling, cool skin, slowed infusion rate, pain. Extravasation (vesicant) = same + burning, blanching, blistering possible.
STOP the infusion immediately. Do NOT remove the IV catheter yet.
Attempt to aspirate residual drug through the catheter (do not irrigate — dilution may spread the drug).
Remove catheter after aspiration attempt.
Mark the area of swelling/redness with a marker. Photograph and measure the affected area.
Notify provider and follow drug-specific protocol for antidote and compress type:
Vesicants with cold compress: anthracyclines (doxorubicin, daunorubicin), mechlorethamine.
Vesicants with warm compress: vinca alkaloids (vincristine, vinblastine), taxanes.
Antidotes: hyaluronidase (vinca alkaloids), sodium thiosulfate (mechlorethamine), DMSO (anthracyclines), phentolamine (vasopressors).
Elevate extremity. Monitor every 15–30 minutes. Refer to plastic surgery/wound care if blistering or necrosis.
Complete incident report. Document size, photo, interventions.
safetyTips: Do NOT apply warm compress to anthracycline extravasation — heat increases local drug toxicity.
Vesicant extravasation can cause full-thickness necrosis requiring surgical debridement — treat aggressively.
Prevention: use central access for vesicants; verify blood return before and during infusion.
keyTakeaways: Stop immediately; aspirate before removing IV
